blocks.p: Percent means per hundred. Every percent question is one of three moves: find a part, find the whole, or find the change. Write the move down before computing.

list: Part: $\text{part} = \frac{\text{percent}}{100} \times \text{whole}$.
Whole: $\text{whole} = \text{part} \div \frac{\text{percent}}{100}$.
Change: $\frac{\text{new}-\text{old}}{\text{old}}\times 100\%$.
Successive percents multiply as decimals: 20% off then 10% off is $0.8\times 0.9=0.72$, not 30% off.
Area and volume scale by the product of the side factors: $0.7\times 1.15=0.805$, so $19.5\%$ smaller.

questions.statement: A department store marks a winter coat, originally priced at $120$, down by $25\%$ for its end-of-season sale. An additional loyalty coupon cannot be combined with sale prices. What does a customer pay for the coat at the sale price?
questions.explain: A 25% discount means paying 75%: $120\times 0.75=90$.

questions.statement: A school newspaper surveys 183 students about the new lunch menu. Of those surveyed, 47 say they prefer the new menu. To the nearest $1\%$, what percent of surveyed students prefer the new menu?
questions.explain: $\frac{47}{183}\times 100\%\approx 25.7\%$, which rounds to $26\%$.

questions.statement: A rectangular garden is redesigned so its length becomes $70\%$ of the original length and its width becomes $115\%$ of the original width. By what percent is the new area smaller than the original area?
questions.explain: Area scales by $0.70\times 1.15=0.805$, so the new area is $80.5\%$ of the old — $19.5\%$ smaller.

questions.statement: An electronics store advertises a laptop originally priced at $200$. At checkout, a $20\%$ coupon is applied first, and then a $10\%$ storewide promotion is applied to the reduced price. What is the final price?
questions.explain: Apply one at a time: $200\times 0.8=160$, then $160\times 0.9=144$. Stacked discounts never simply add.

questions.statement: After her annual review, Priya's salary increases from $52{,}000$ dollars to $58{,}900$ dollars. To the nearest tenth of a percent, what was the percent increase?

A restaurant bill totals $64$ dollars before tax. The local sales tax is $8\%$, and the diners leave an $18\%$ tip calculated on the pre-tax bill. What is the total amount paid, including tax and tip?

A salesperson earns $6\%$ commission on the first $50{,}000$ dollars of sales and $9\%$ on any amount above that. If her total sales for the month are $80{,}000$ dollars, how much commission does she earn?
A town's population of $12{,}000$ falls by $15\%$ one year and then rises by $15\%$ the next year. What is the population after the two changes?
questions.explain: $12{,}000\times 0.85\times 1.15=12{,}000\times 0.9775=11{,}730$. Equal percent moves do not cancel — the base changes.

questions.statement: A chemist has $40$ liters of a $15\%$ acid solution. She adds $10$ liters of pure water. What percent of the new mixture is acid?
questions.explain: Acid stays $0.15(40)=6$ liters while volume becomes $50$ liters: $\frac{6}{50}=12\%$.

questions.statement: After receiving a $12\%$ raise, an employee now earns $61{,}600$ dollars. What was the salary before the raise?
questions.explain: Divide by what was paid: $61{,}600\div 1.12=55{,}000$. Never subtract $12\%$ of the new salary.

blocks.p: A ratio compares quantities with the same units. A proportion sets two ratios equal. Nearly every ACT ratio word problem is one of four moves: split a total by parts, scale by a unit rate, cross-multiply a proportion, or flip it for inverse proportion. Name the move before you compute.

list: Parts split: divide the total by the sum of the parts to get one part, then multiply by each share.
Unit rate: shrink everything to a per-one rate first, then scale up to the target quantity.
Proportion: $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}$ cross-multiplies to $ad=bc$. Map scales live here.
Three-part chains: rescale both ratios so the shared middle term matches, then read the chain straight across.

blocks.p: Scale and similarity are proportions in costume. Length scale $k$ means area scales by $k^2$ and volume by $k^3$ — always square or cube the ratio, never carry it straight. Forgetting this step is the number-one hard-question trap.

list: Direct grows together; inverse multiplies to a fixed total — workers times days stays constant no matter the crew size.
Mixtures: track the pure amount, never the percent — adding water later never changes the pure quantity.
Percent-ratio hybrids: turn the percent into a keep-ratio first (keep-rate versus off-rate), then apply it like any ratio.

questions.statement: A summer program enrolls $32$ students, and the ratio of boys to girls is $5{:}3$. The counselors want equal-sized activity groups with no mixing across cabins. How many boys are enrolled?
questions.explain: Total parts $5+3=8$; one part is $32\div 8=4$. Boys: $5\times 4=20$. A picks the girls; D divides by the wrong part.

questions.statement: A highway map uses a scale of $1$ inch to $25$ miles. A family measures the route between two rest stops as $3.6$ inches on the map. They drive at a steady $60$ mph. How many miles long is that stretch?
questions.explain: Proportion: $3.6\times 25=90$ miles. The $60$ mph is decoration — the question asks for miles, not hours.

questions.statement: A bakery keeps its flour-to-sugar ratio at $5{:}2$ for a signature loaf. A morning batch uses $15$ cups of flour because of a bulk delivery. How many cups of sugar does that batch require?
questions.explain: One flour part is $15\div 5=3$ cups, so sugar is $2\times 3=6$ cups. C scales by $1.5$ instead of the part value.

questions.statement: A delivery van travels $420$ miles on $15$ gallons of gas. The dispatcher assigns a $196$-mile route tomorrow and wants the exact fuel needed at the same efficiency. How many gallons are required?
questions.explain: Unit rate $420\div 15=28$ mpg. Then $196\div 28=7$ gallons. Reduce to one unit first, then scale up.

questions.statement: Three volunteers split a $240$ prize in the ratio $2{:}3{:}5$ based on hours worked. The organizer hands each share in cash. What is the smallest share?
questions.explain: Total parts $10$; one part $240\div 10=24$. Smallest: $2\times 24=48$. D is the middle share, not the smallest.

questions.statement: Two rectangular garden plots are similar, with side lengths in the ratio $3{:}5$. The smaller plot has area $54$ square meters. A landscaper prices sod by area. What is the area of the larger plot?
questions.explain: Area ratio is $3^2{:}5^2=9{:}25$. One area part is $54\div 9=6$, so larger is $25\times 6=150$. A scales linearly and forgets to square.

questions.statement: A crew of $6$ painters finishes a warehouse in $12$ days working at the same pace. The deadline moves up, so the foreman raises the crew to $9$ painters at the same pace. How many days will the job take now?
questions.explain: Worker-days constant: $6\times 12=72$. Then $72\div 9=8$ days. More workers means fewer days — direct division $12\div 9$ is the trap.

questions.statement: A lab mixes acid and water in the ratio $3{:}2$ to make $45$ liters of cleaning solution. An inspector tests the acid content only. How many liters of acid are in the batch?
questions.explain: Total parts $5$; one part $45\div 5=9$. Acid: $3\times 9=27$ L. A is the water share.

questions.statement: A $144{,}000$ grant is divided among three labs in the ratio $2{:}3{:}7$. The middle lab spends its share on equipment. How much does the middle lab receive?
questions.explain: Total parts $12$; one part $144{,}000\div 12=12{,}000$. Middle: $3\times 12{,}000=36{,}000$. D is the largest share.

questions.statement: An architect's floor plan uses $1$ cm to $4$ m. A conference room measures $3.25$ cm by $4.5$ cm on the plan. The client wants the real floor area for carpet. What is it, in square meters?
questions.explain: Real sides: $3.25\times 4=13$ m and $4.5\times 4=18$ m. Area $13\times 18=234$. A multiplies plan area by $4$ once instead of scaling each side.

questions.statement: Two laptops sell in the price ratio $4{:}7$. The expensive model costs $21$ more than the basic model during a sale. What is the price of the basic model?
questions.explain: Gap parts $7-4=3$ equal $21$, so one part is $7$. Basic: $4\times 7=28$. D is the expensive model.

questions.statement: Two freight trains leave a yard at the same time on parallel tracks, with speeds in the ratio $5{:}8$. After the same travel time, the faster train is $45$ miles ahead. A dispatcher needs the slower train's distance. How far has it traveled?
questions.explain: Gap parts $3$ equal $45$ miles, so one part is $15$. Slower: $5\times 15=75$ miles. Equal times mean distances share the speed ratio.

questions.statement: A foundry casts an alloy with copper and zinc in the ratio $7{:}5$. A crucible holds $42$ kg of copper for a pour. How many kilograms of zinc must be added to keep the ratio?
questions.explain: One copper part is $42\div 7=6$ kg, so zinc is $5\times 6=30$ kg. Cross-multiplying $7/5=42/z$ gives the same $z=30$.

questions.statement: A contractor mixes red, blue, and white paint in the ratio $4{:}3{:}1$ for $24$ gallons of custom color. The supplier runs short on blue pigment. How many gallons of blue paint does the full order need?
questions.explain: Total parts $8$; one part $24\div 8=3$ gallons. Blue: $3\times 3=9$ gallons. D doubles the blue parts.

questions.statement: A robotics club starts with boys and girls in the ratio $3{:}5$. Then $8$ new girls join and no boys join, making the ratio $1{:}2$. The advisor needs the original boy count for uniforms. How many boys were there at the start?
questions.explain: Let parts be $k$: $3k/(5k+8)=1/2$, so $6k=5k+8$ and $k=8$. Boys: $3\times 8=24$. Check: $24$ to $48$ is $1{:}2$.

questions.statement: Two delivery trucks travel for the same time with speeds in the ratio $7{:}9$. The faster truck covers $36$ miles more than the slower one. How many miles does the slower truck cover?
questions.explain: Gap parts $2$ equal $36$ miles, so one part is $18$. Slower: $7\times 18=126$ miles. Same time means distance ratio equals speed ratio.

questions.statement: A pastry chef holds flour, sugar, and butter in the ratio $6{:}4{:}3$. A holiday order uses $2.5$ cups of sugar. How many cups of flour does it need?
questions.explain: One sugar part is $2.5\div 4=0.625$ cups. Flour: $6\times 0.625=3.75$ cups. B rounds the part value early.

questions.statement: A trail map has scale $1{:}50{,}000$. A scout measures $8.4$ cm between two camps on the map. The troop hikes in kilometers. What is the real distance?
questions.explain: Real cm: $8.4\times 50{,}000=420{,}000$ cm $=4{,}200$ m $=4.2$ km. C misses the cm-to-km conversion ($100{,}000$ cm per km).

questions.statement: Two bottling machines run together with output rates in the ratio $3{:}2$, producing $30$ bottles per minute combined. An engineer isolates the faster machine for testing. How many bottles per minute does it produce alone?
questions.explain: Total parts $5$; one part $30\div 5=6$. Faster: $3\times 6=18$ per minute. A is the slower machine.

questions.statement: Four identical pumps drain a flooded basement in $9$ hours. The crew brings in two more identical pumps, for $6$ total, all at the same rate. How long will draining take now?
questions.explain: Pump-hours constant: $4\times 9=36$. Then $36\div 6=6$ hours. D divides the wrong direction.

questions.statement: Three assembly lines produce at rates in the ratio $2{:}3{:}4$, with $1{,}080$ units total in a shift. Quality control audits the fastest line's full output. How many units is that?
questions.explain: Total parts $9$; one part $1{,}080\div 9=120$. Fastest: $4\times 120=480$ units. A is the slowest line.

questions.statement: Two similar storage cubes have edge lengths in the ratio $2{:}3$. The smaller cube holds $64$ cubic feet. The buyer wants the larger cube's capacity. What is it?
questions.explain: Volume ratio is $2^3{:}3^3=8{:}27$. One part is $64\div 8=8$, so larger is $27\times 8=216$. B scales by area ($4{:}9$) instead of volume.

questions.statement: A chemist has $15$ liters of $20\%$ salt solution and adds some $50\%$ solution to reach a $30\%$ mixture. She tracks pure salt only. How many liters of $50\%$ solution must she add?
A shelter starts with dogs and cats in the ratio $5{:}3$. After $12$ dogs are adopted and no cats leave, the ratio becomes $1{:}1$. How many cats are there?
questions.explain: Let $k$ be the part: $5k-12=3k$, so $2k=12$ and $k=6$. Cats: $3\times 6=18$. Verify: $30-12=18$ dogs equals $18$ cats.

questions.statement: Two cyclists start together on a $60$-mile charity ride at steady speeds of $16$ mph and $20$ mph. The organizer at the finish wants the gap between them when the faster rider finishes. How many miles behind is the slower rider then?
questions.explain: Faster takes $60\div 20=3$ hr. Slower covers $16\times 3=48$ miles, so the gap is $60-48=12$ miles. C uses a $2.5$-hr guess instead of the true $3$-hr time.

questions.statement: Two meshed gears have teeth in the ratio $8{:}5$ (large to small). The large gear turns $120$ times during a test run. Because rotations run inverse to teeth, how many times does the small gear turn?
questions.explain: Rotations ratio is $5{:}8$. Small turns $120\times 8\div 5=192$ times. A multiplies by $5/8$ instead of flipping.

questions.statement: A bank exchanges dollars to euros at $1=0.90$ euros, then charges a $2\%$ fee on the euro amount. A traveler exchanges $500$ for a homestay deposit. How many euros does she receive?
questions.explain: Gross euros: $500\times 0.90=450$. After the fee keep $98\%$: $450\times 0.98=441$. C forgets the fee.

questions.statement: A $6$-foot pole casts a $9$-foot shadow. At the same time, a courthouse casts a $51$-foot shadow. A surveyor needs the courthouse height. What is it, in feet?
questions.explain: Same sun angle: $6/9=h/51$, so $h=51\times 6\div 9=34$ ft. B flips a ratio.

questions.statement: Three funds hold money with $A{:}B=3{:}4$ and $B{:}C=5{:}6$. An auditor finds $45{,}000$ in fund A. How much is in fund C?
A $2.5$-kg brine has salt and water in the ratio $1{:}9$ by mass. A cook adds $0.5$ kg of pure water for soup stock. What percent of the new mixture is salt?
questions.explain: Salt stays $2.5\div 10=0.25$ kg; new total $3.0$ kg. Percent: $0.25\div 3.0\approx 8.33\%$. A divides by $3.125$ instead of $3.0$.

blocks.p: Every rate problem is distance equals rate times time, or work equals rate times time. Write the equation with units attached before touching numbers. If the units on the two sides do not match, convert first — the ACT plants one answer that skips the conversion.

list: Distance: $d=rt$. Average speed is total distance over total time — never the average of two speeds.
Same-distance round trip: $v_{avg}=\frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ — the answer always lands below the plain average of the two speeds.
Work: add each worker's per-hour fraction of one job, then flip the total rate to get the shared time.
Drain opposes fill: subtract the drain's fraction from the fill's fraction, then flip the net rate for the true time.

blocks.p: Current and wind split into two equations: downstream adds, upstream subtracts. Boat $b$ with current $c$ gives $b+c$ one way and $b-c$ back. Add the equations to kill $c$; subtract to kill $b$.

list: Meeting head-on: add both speeds into one closing speed, then divide the starting gap by it.
Conversions: multiply by $1$ in disguise and cancel units — memorize the mph, gallon, and km/h factors so the setup is automatic.
Area converts squared and volume cubed — square feet become square yards by dividing by $9$. Dosage scales by proportion: keep mg over mL equal on both sides.

questions.statement: A charter jet covers $1{,}350$ miles in $3$ hours at a steady cruising speed. The airline schedules the same route daily. What is the jet's average speed in miles per hour?
questions.explain: $d=rt$ gives $r=1{,}350\div 3=450$ mph. D divides by $2.5$ instead of $3$.

questions.statement: A traffic engineer converts speed limits to feet per second for a sensor system. A test car travels at $66$ mph. Using $1$ mph $=\frac{22}{15}$ ft/s, what is the car's speed in ft/s?
questions.explain: $66\times 22\div 15=1{,}452\div 15=96.8$ ft/s. A converts $60$ mph instead of $66$.

questions.statement: A salesman drives to a client at $60$ mph and returns by the same route at $40$ mph because of traffic. His expense form asks for the average speed for the whole trip. What should he report?
questions.explain: Same distance $d$: total time $d/60+d/40=5d/120$, so $v=2d\div 5d/120=48$ mph. D averages the speeds and ignores the extra time at $40$.

questions.statement: Maya proofreads a manuscript alone in $6$ hours and Leo alone in $3$ hours. They split the same manuscript and work together at their usual paces. How long will it take them?
questions.explain: Rates add: $1/6+1/3=1/2$ job per hour, so $T=2$ hours. D averages the times instead of the rates.

questions.statement: A pool inlet fills the pool in $8$ hours while a drain empties it in $12$ hours. The crew leaves both open by mistake starting from an empty pool. How long until the pool fills?
questions.explain: Net rate $1/8-1/12=1/24$ pool per hour, so $24$ hours. B adds the rates as if both fill.

questions.statement: Two hikers start $30$ miles apart on a trail and walk toward each other at $8$ mph and $12$ mph. A ranger wants to know when their paths cross. After how many hours do they meet?
questions.explain: Closing speed $8+12=20$ mph; time $30\div 20=1.5$ hr. C divides by one speed only.

questions.statement: A ferry's downstream speed is $24$ mph and its upstream speed on the same stretch is $16$ mph. The captain logs the river's current speed. What is it?
questions.explain: Subtract: $(b+c)-(b-c)=2c=8$, so $c=4$ mph. Boat speed is $20$ mph. A halves once too often.

questions.statement: A sprinter runs $5$ km in $12$ minutes during a tempo workout. Her coach records the pace in meters per second. What is her average speed?
questions.explain: $5{,}000$ m over $720$ s: $5{,}000\div 720\approx 6.94$ m/s. A divides kilometers by seconds without converting.

questions.statement: Machine A bottles $50$ cases per hour and machine B bottles $30$ per hour. A runs alone for the first $2$ hours of a shift, then both run together for $3$ more hours. How many cases are bottled in the shift?
questions.explain: A alone: $50\times 5=250$ total for A; B adds $30\times 3=90$. Total $340$. D runs both for all $5$ hours.

questions.statement: An airport walkway moves at $120$ ft/min. A traveler walks the same direction at $80$ ft/min relative to the walkway during a $400$-foot ride. How fast does she move relative to the floor?
questions.explain: Same direction adds: $120+80=200$ ft/min. A subtracts as if she walked backward.

questions.statement: A generator manual lists fuel in liters, but the tank is marked in gallons ($1$ gal $=3.785$ L). A technician pours $12$ gallons into an empty tank. How many liters is that?
questions.explain: $12\times 3.785=45.42$ L. A divides instead of multiplying.

questions.statement: Printer A prints $30$ pages per minute and printer B prints $20$ per minute. An office runs both together on a $1{,}000$-page report. How many minutes will the job take?
questions.explain: Combined $50$ ppm; $1{,}000\div 50=20$ min. D uses one printer only.

questions.statement: Two trains leave stations $600$ miles apart heading toward each other at $90$ mph and $110$ mph. Dispatch needs the meeting time. After how many hours do they meet?
questions.explain: Closing $200$ mph; $600\div 200=3$ hr. D divides by one speed.

questions.statement: A driver covers $120$ miles at $60$ mph, stops $30$ minutes for lunch, then covers $60$ more miles at $40$ mph. Her log needs the average speed including the stop. What is it?
questions.explain: Drive time $2+1.5=3.5$ hr plus $0.5$ stop $=4$ hr; distance $180$ miles. $180\div 4=45$ mph. D drops the stop.

questions.statement: Three interns file a archive alone in $6$, $8$, and $12$ hours respectively. They share one archive equally at their usual paces. How long will it take them together?
questions.explain: Rate $1/6+1/8+1/12=9/24=3/8$ per hour, so $T=8/3$ hr $=2$ hr $40$ min. C averages the times.

questions.statement: Two hoses fill a $480$-gallon tank at $4$ and $6$ gallons per minute. The groundskeeper opens both on an empty tank. How many minutes will it take?
questions.explain: Combined $10$ gpm; $480\div 10=48$ min. D uses one hose.

questions.statement: A plane with airspeed $300$ mph flies $600$ miles out against a $50$-mph headwind and returns with a $50$-mph tailwind. How long is the round trip, in hours?
questions.explain: Out $600\div 250=2.4$ hr; back $600\div 350\approx 1.71$ hr. Total $\approx 4.11$ hr. B ignores the wind.

questions.statement: A bedroom measures $12$ ft by $15$ ft. Carpet is sold by the square yard. How many square yards does the room need?
questions.explain: $180$ sq ft $\div 9=20$ sq yd. D reports square feet.

questions.statement: A syrup contains $250$ mg of medicine per $5$ mL. A prescription calls for $375$ mg. The pharmacist measures the matching volume. How many milliliters is the dose?
questions.explain: Proportion $250/5=375/x$ gives $x=7.5$ mL. A scales by $1.5$ on the wrong quantity.

questions.statement: Painter A paints a house alone in $4$ hours and painter B alone in $6$ hours. A works alone for $1$ hour, then B joins. How much longer after B joins will they take to finish?
questions.explain: A finishes $1/4$; $3/4$ remains. Combined rate $1/4+1/6=5/12$ per hour. Time $(3/4)\div(5/12)=9/5=1.8$ hr. D restarts the whole job.

questions.statement: A tour boat cruises at $16$ mph in still water through a $4$-mph current. A tour runs downstream and back for $6$ hours of cruising with no stops. How far one way is the turnaround point?
questions.explain: Speeds $20$ down, $12$ up: $d/20+d/12=6$, so $8d/60=6$ and $d=45$ miles. B averages the speeds.

questions.statement: A sorting belt moves at $2.5$ ft/s. A package stays on the belt for $40$ seconds from load to diverter. How many feet down the line is the diverter?
questions.explain: $d=2.5\times 40=100$ ft. A multiplies by $32$ instead of $40$.

questions.statement: A jet burns $900$ gallons per hour. Dispatch plans a $5$-hour flight plus a $20\%$ fuel reserve over the trip burn. How many gallons must be loaded?
questions.explain: Trip burn $900\times 5=4{,}500$; reserve factor $1.2$ gives $5{,}400$ gallons. A skips the reserve.

questions.statement: Ann types $60$ words per minute and Ben types $40$ per minute. They split a $5{,}000$-word transcript and type together. How many minutes will it take?
questions.explain: Combined $100$ wpm; $5{,}000\div 100=50$ min. D uses Ben alone.

questions.statement: A sprinter runs $100$ m in $9.8$ seconds in a time trial. Analysts quote top speed in km/h. What is her average speed in km/h?
questions.explain: $100\div 9.8\approx 10.2$ m/s; times $3.6$ gives $\approx 36.7$ km/h. A forgets the m/s-to-km/h factor.

questions.statement: Pump A fills a tank alone in $10$ minutes and pump B alone in $15$ minutes. The operator alternates them each minute starting with A. How many minutes until the tank is full?
questions.explain: Each $2$-min cycle adds $1/10+1/15=1/6$ of a tank. Six cycles ($12$ min) complete it exactly. C assumes a partial final cycle.

questions.statement: A kayaker paddles $24$ miles downstream at $12$ mph, stops $1$ hour for lunch, then returns $24$ miles upstream at $4$ mph. What is the total trip time including the stop?
questions.explain: Down $24\div 12=2$ hr; up $24\div 4=6$ hr; plus $1$ hr stop $=9$ hr. B drops the lunch hour.

questions.statement: A lab connection downloads at $50$ megabits per second. A dataset is $1.5$ gigabytes ($1$ byte $=8$ bits). About how long will the download take?
questions.explain: Bits: $1.5\times 8=12$ gigabits $=12{,}000$ Mb. Time $12{,}000\div 50=240$ s $=4$ min. A divides gigabytes by megabits directly.

questions.statement: Three hoses fill a cistern alone in $6$, $8$, and $12$ hours. The keeper opens all three on an empty cistern. How long until it fills?
questions.explain: Rate $1/6+1/8+1/12=9/24=3/8$ per hour, so $T=8/3$ hr $=2$ hr $40$ min. D adds the times.

questions.statement: A marathoner passes $10$ km at $40$ minutes and finishes the $42.195$-km race in $3$ hours flat. Her coach wants her average speed after the $10$-km mark. What is it, in km/h?
questions.explain: Remaining $32.195$ km in $140$ min ($7/3$ hr): $32.195\div 7/3\approx 13.8$ km/h. C divides the full distance by the split time.

blocks.p: Every mean question runs through the total: average times count. When a value joins, leaves, or is still unknown, rebuild the total first and let the average follow — never average the averages.

list: Total-first: $\text{total}=\text{average}\times\text{count}$. New average means new total divided by new count.
Missing value: target total minus the sum you already have. Set up target times count before subtracting.
Removing entries: subtract their sum from the old total, then divide by the smaller count.
Consecutive integers are symmetric — the mean sits exactly on the middle term.

blocks.p: Weighted average gives louder voices to bigger groups: each value times its weight, summed, over all weights. Money models work the same way — fixed costs spread over units while per-unit margins stack.

list: Weight by the right thing: headcounts, kilograms, credits, or dollars — never by the values themselves.
Percent weights must total a whole before you trust the blend.
Break-even: fixed cost divided by per-unit margin. Below it you lose, above it you earn.
Scoring systems (+points/−penalty): translate the total score and the answered count into two equations.

questions.statement: After five exams, Nadia's average is $82$. Her scholarship requires an average of $85$ across six exams. Her advisor asks what she must score on the sixth exam. What does she need?
questions.explain: Needed $=85\cdot 6-82\cdot 5=510-410=100$. Total-first, then subtract.

questions.statement: A hiking club has $8$ members with an average age of $24$. Two new members, both age $30$, join before a trip. The roster needs the new average age. What is it?
questions.explain: New total $(8\cdot 24+60)\div 10=252\div 10=25.2$. Never average $24$ and $30$ directly.

questions.statement: A course weights the midterm $40\%$ and the final $60\%$. Omar scores $88$ on the midterm and $94$ on the final. What is his course average?
questions.explain: $0.4(88)+0.6(94)=35.2+56.4=91.6$. The heavier weight pulls toward the final.

questions.statement: A grocer blends $20$ kg of peanuts at $6$ per kg with $30$ kg of cashews at $9$ per kg. The label needs the blend's price per kilogram. What is it?
questions.explain: $(20\cdot 6+30\cdot 9)\div 50=390\div 50=7.8$. Weight by kilograms, not by prices.

questions.statement: Seven consecutive integers have an average of $41$. A puzzle asks for the largest of the seven. What is it?
questions.explain: The mean is the middle term ($41$); three steps up gives $44$. Symmetry does the work.

questions.statement: Ten lab readings average $60$, but the technician discovers one faulty reading of $100$ and discards it. What is the average of the remaining nine readings?
questions.explain: $(10\cdot 60-100)\div 9=500\div 9\approx 55.56$. Rebuild the total, then divide by nine.

questions.statement: A workshop charges $13$ per ticket, costs $8$ per attendee in materials, and pays $500$ hall rent. The organizer needs the break-even attendance. How many tickets is that?
questions.explain: Margin $5$ per ticket; $500\div 5=100$. Fixed cost over per-unit margin.

questions.statement: A gadget sells for $45$ with a $28$ unit cost plus $3{,}400$ in fixed costs. A retailer orders $500$ units and finance wants the profit. What is it?
questions.explain: $(45-28)\cdot 500-3{,}400=8{,}500-3{,}400=5{,}100$. Margin stacks, fixed subtracts once.

questions.statement: A warehouse pays $12$ workers an average of $18$ per hour and $8$ workers an average of $24$ per hour. Payroll needs the combined average wage. What is it?
questions.explain: $(12\cdot 18+8\cdot 24)\div 20=408\div 20=20.40$. Weight by headcount.

questions.statement: After three quizzes averaging $78$, Priya has two quizzes left and targets an $82$ average across all five. What must she average on the final two quizzes?
questions.explain: $(82\cdot 5-78\cdot 3)\div 2=(410-234)\div 2=88$. Target total minus banked total, split over two.

questions.statement: An investor holds $4{,}000$ at $6\%$ and $6{,}000$ at $4\%$. Her statement shows a single blended rate. What is it?
Six numbers have a mean of $20$, and three of them sum to $45$. A researcher needs the average of the other three. What is it?
questions.explain: Leftover total $120-45=75$ over three numbers: $25$. Totals first, always.

questions.statement: A $25$-question contest awards $4$ points per correct answer and subtracts $1$ per wrong answer, with blanks scoring zero. Sam leaves $5$ blank and finishes with $55$ points. How many did he answer wrong?
questions.explain: With $c+w=20$ and $4c-w=55$, adding gives $5c=75$, so $c=15$ and $w=5$.

questions.statement: A rep earns $2{,}000$ base plus $8\%$ of sales above $10{,}000$. Her paycheck totals $3{,}200$. What were her total sales?
questions.explain: Excess pay $1{,}200\div 0.08=15{,}000$ over threshold, so sales $=25{,}000$. Split base from commission first.

questions.statement: A survey records values $3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9$. The analyst reports the mean. What is it, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: Total $43$ over $7$ entries: $43\div 7\approx 6.14$. Count repeats individually.

questions.statement: Eight boxes average $25$ kg. Two boxes averaging $20$ kg are shipped out. What is the average weight of the remaining six boxes?
questions.explain: $(8\cdot 25-2\cdot 20)\div 6=160\div 6\approx 26.67$. Removing below-average boxes lifts the mean.

questions.statement: Plan A costs $50$ plus $0.20$ per mile; Plan B is a flat $80$. A courier wants the mileage where both plans cost the same. How many miles is that?
questions.explain: Gap $30\div 0.20=150$ miles. Set the cost expressions equal.

questions.statement: A yard melts $3$ kg of scrap at $12$ per kg with $7$ kg at $18$ per kg. What is the average cost per kilogram of the melt?
questions.explain: $(3\cdot 12+7\cdot 18)\div 10=162\div 10=16.2$. The heavier portion dominates.

questions.statement: In a class, $20$ boys average $75$ and $30$ girls average $85$. The school reports one class average. What is it?
questions.explain: $(20\cdot 75+30\cdot 85)\div 50=4{,}050\div 50=81$. Closer to the girls' mean, as expected.

questions.statement: Luis has test scores of $88, 92,$ and $86$ and needs a $90$ average across four tests for an exemption. What must he score on the fourth test?
questions.explain: $90\cdot 4-(88+92+86)=360-266=94$. Target total minus banked sum.

questions.statement: Five employees average $60{,}000$. The firm hires one specialist at $90{,}000$. What is the new average salary?
A stand sells $40$ jars at $25$ and $60$ jars at $30$ during a festival. What is the average revenue per jar?
questions.explain: $(40\cdot 25+60\cdot 30)\div 100=2{,}800\div 100=28$. Weight by jars sold.

questions.statement: A phone plan charges $30$ for $500$ minutes plus $0.10$ per extra minute. June's bill is $47$. How many minutes were used in total?
questions.explain: Overage $(47-30)\div 0.10=170$ minutes beyond $500$, so $670$ total. Add the base back.

questions.statement: A roaster blends $5$ kg at $14$ per kg with $3$ kg at $22$ per kg for a house mix. What is the mix's cost per kilogram?
Scores of $70, 80, 85, 90, 95$ are recorded, and the lowest is dropped before averaging. What is the resulting average?
questions.explain: $(80+85+90+95)\div 4=350\div 4=87.5$. Drop first, then divide by four.

questions.statement: Factory A makes $200$ units a day for $30$ days; Factory B makes $300$ a day for $20$ days. What is the combined average daily output?
questions.explain: Total $(6{,}000+6{,}000)\div 50=240$ units a day. Weight by days, not by factories.

questions.statement: A saver deposits $9{,}000$ across two accounts at $4\%$ and $6\%$, earning $460$ in a year. How much sits in the $6\%$ account?
A taxi charges a $3$ flag fee plus $2.50$ per mile. A ride costs $28$. How many miles long was the ride?
questions.explain: $(28-3)\div 2.50=10$ miles. Strip the flag before dividing.

questions.statement: Homework at $95$ counts $20\%$, quizzes at $80$ count $30\%$, and the exam counts $50\%$. Mia wants an $85$ overall. What exam score does she need?
Five consecutive even integers have an average of $30$. A contest asks for the largest. What is it?
questions.explain: The mean is the middle even ($30$); two steps of two give $34$.

blocks.p: Exponents count repeated multiplication, so same-base powers combine instead of expanding. Name which rule each factor needs — product, quotient, or power — and apply it once per base.

list: Multiplying same bases adds exponents; dividing subtracts them.
A power raised to a power multiplies exponents — watch whether the exponent sits inside or outside.
Any nonzero base to the zero power equals one.
Negative exponents flip into reciprocals before any other move.

blocks.p: Scientific notation separates size from precision: one nonzero digit, then a power of ten. Growth and decay are exponents in disguise — repeated doubling, tripling, or halving over equal steps.

list: Normalize first: exactly one nonzero digit left of the decimal point.
Multiplying or dividing: handle the front numbers and the tens separately, then recombine.
Adding or subtracting requires matching exponents — shift one term until they agree.
Repeated change over equal intervals is a power: doubling, tripling, and halving each carry their own base.

questions.statement: A petri dish starts with $500$ bacteria that double every hour. A technician checks the dish $6$ hours later. How many bacteria are present?
questions.explain: $500\cdot 2^6=500\cdot 64=32{,}000$. Doubling six times is a factor of $2^6$, not $2\cdot 6$.

questions.statement: A filter traps particles as small as $0.0000045$ meters. The report requires scientific notation. Which form is correct?
questions.explain: Move the decimal six places right: $4.5\times 10^{-6}$. B has two digits left of the point; A miscounts the shift.

questions.statement: A sheet $0.1$ mm thick is folded in half $20$ times, doubling its thickness each fold. A journalist wants the final thickness in meters. About how thick is the stack?
questions.explain: $0.1\cdot 2^{20}=104{,}857.6$ mm $\approx 104.9$ m. Then convert millimeters to meters — skipping the conversion gives D.

questions.statement: A backup of $5\times 10^9$ bytes moves at $2\times 10^5$ bytes per second. The admin needs the transfer time in seconds. How long will it take?
questions.explain: Divide mantissas and subtract tens: $5\div 2=2.5$, $10^{9-5}=10^4$. D multiplies the tens instead.

questions.statement: A patient receives $240$ mg of a tracer that halves every hour. Imaging happens $3$ hours after injection. How much tracer remains?
questions.explain: Three halvings divide by $2^3=8$: $240\div 8=30$ mg. A divides by $3$ instead of $2^3$.

questions.statement: A savings account holds $2{,}000$ at $5\%$ annual compound interest. The owner checks the balance after $2$ years with no deposits or withdrawals. What is it?
questions.explain: $2{,}000\cdot 1.05^2=2{,}000\cdot 1.1025=2{,}205$. Simple interest ($2{,}200$) misses compounding on the first year's gain.

questions.statement: A sample holds $10^5$ cells per mL, then is diluted $100$-fold for counting. The protocol needs the new concentration as a power of ten. What is it?
questions.explain: Dividing by $10^2$ subtracts exponents: $10^{5-2}=10^3$. C adds instead of subtracting.

questions.statement: A cubic storage tank has edges $3\times 10^2$ meters long. The manifest needs its volume in scientific notation. What is the volume, in cubic meters?
questions.explain: Cube the mantissa and triple the ten: $3^3\times 10^6=27\times 10^6=2.7\times 10^7$. Then normalize to one leading digit.

questions.statement: Four data centers report capacity as $2^{10}$, $10^3$, $3^6$, and $5^4$ terabytes. An analyst needs the largest. Which is greatest?
questions.explain: $2^{10}=1{,}024$ beats $1{,}000$, $729$, and $625$. Compare values, never bases or exponents alone.

questions.statement: A reservoir covers $4\times 10^6$ square meters at an average depth of $2.5\times 10^{-3}$ meters after a dry spell. What volume of water remains, in cubic meters?
questions.explain: Multiply mantissas ($4\cdot 2.5=10$) and add tens ($6-3=3$): $10\times 10^3=1.0\times 10^4$. Normalize at the end.

questions.statement: A fundraiser starts with $3$ volunteers, and each volunteer recruits $3$ more, repeating for $4$ additional rounds. How many volunteers join in the final round?
questions.explain: Round counts run $3^1$ through $3^5$; the fifth round is $243$. Off-by-one on rounds gives A.

questions.statement: A lab stores $800$ g of an isotope with a $10$-year half-life. Safety rules ask for the amount remaining after $30$ years. How much is left?
questions.explain: $30$ years is three half-lives: $800\div 2^3=100$ g. Count intervals, not years.

questions.statement: A system defines $1$ GB as $2^{30}$ bytes. A technician installs an $8$-GB module and logs its capacity as a single power of two. What should she write?
questions.explain: $8\cdot 2^{30}=2^3\cdot 2^{30}=2^{33}$. Multiplying same bases adds exponents.

questions.statement: A script can evaluate $(2^3)^2$ or $2^{(3^2)}$ for a key size. The engineer picks the larger value. Which expression wins?
questions.explain: $(2^3)^2=2^6=64$ while $2^{(3^2)}=2^9=512$. A stacked exponent is not the same as a multiplied one.

questions.statement: A square garden's side length quadruples during an expansion, and the new area is $256$ square meters. The deed needs the original side length. What was it?
questions.explain: Area scales by $4^2=16$, so old area is $16$ and old side is $4$ m. B takes the square root of the new area directly.

questions.statement: A cubic tank's volume grows by a factor of $8$ after an upgrade, reaching edges of $10$ m. What was the original edge length?
questions.explain: Volume $\times 8$ means edges $\times\sqrt[3]{8}=2$, so old edge is $5$ m. Volume factors cube the edge factor.

questions.statement: A telescope's light gathering scales as the square of its mirror diameter. An observatory triples its mirror diameter. By what factor does light gathering increase?
questions.explain: The square of $3$ is $9$. C cubes instead of squaring.

questions.statement: A probe's signal strength falls as the inverse square of its distance. Controllers move it twice as far away. What fraction of the original signal remains?
questions.explain: $1\div 2^2=1/4$ remains. C uses an inverse instead of an inverse square.

questions.statement: A label lists a concentration of $7.2\times 10^{-4}$ grams per mL. A nurse's chart needs the plain decimal. What should she write?
questions.explain: Shift the point four places left: $0.00072$. A shifts only three.

questions.statement: A project combines grants of $3\times 10^5$ and $7\times 10^4$ dollars. Finance needs the total in scientific notation. What is it?
questions.explain: Align tens first: $3.0\times 10^5+0.7\times 10^5=3.7\times 10^5$. Adding mantissas with mismatched tens gives D.

questions.statement: A metro area has $8.5\times 10^6$ residents, and $2.5\times 10^5$ live outside the transit zone. How many live inside it?
questions.explain: $8.50\times 10^6-0.25\times 10^6=8.25\times 10^6$. Align to the larger ten before subtracting.

questions.statement: An engineer estimates $(6.1\times 10^3)(9.8\times 10^4)$ for a parts order. Which estimate is closest?
questions.explain: $6.1\cdot 9.8\approx 60$, tens $10^7$: $\approx 6.0\times 10^8$. A drops a ten.

questions.statement: A contest asks for the units digit of $3^{20}$. The pattern of final digits cycles every four powers. What is the digit?
questions.explain: Powers of $3$ end $3{,}9{,}7{,}1$ repeating; the $20$th (multiple of $4$) ends in $1$.

questions.statement: A mold colony of $100$ spores triples every $2$ hours in an incubator. A researcher opens it $6$ hours later. How many spores are there?
questions.explain: Three tripling intervals: $100\cdot 3^3=2{,}700$. B multiplies by $3\cdot 3$ instead of $3^3$.

questions.statement: A delivery van worth $1{,}200$ loses $10\%$ of its value each year. The fleet manager values it after $2$ years. What is it worth?
questions.explain: $1{,}200\cdot 0.9^2=1{,}200\cdot 0.81=972$. Subtracting $20\%$ flat gives A.

questions.statement: A cistern first loses one-eighth of its water to a leak, then one-quarter of the original volume to irrigation. What fraction of the original water is gone?
questions.explain: Same-original fractions add: $1/8+2/8=3/8$. B compounds the second loss on the remainder.

questions.statement: A square sensor has sides $5\times 10^{-2}$ meters. The spec sheet needs its area in scientific notation. What is the area, in square meters?
questions.explain: Square mantissa and double the ten: $25\times 10^{-4}=2.5\times 10^{-3}$. B never normalizes.

questions.statement: A culture holds $2^6$ cells and a centrifuge concentrates it by removing a divisor of $2^{-2}$. The log needs the final count as a power of two. What is it?
questions.explain: Dividing by $2^{-2}$ adds two: $2^{6-(-2)}=2^8=256$. A subtracts the wrong direction.

questions.statement: A fractal patch's area equals $16$ raised to the $3/4$ power square units. The survey needs the numeric area. What is it?
questions.explain: Fourth root first ($2$), then cube: $2^3=8$. C takes the root but forgets the power.

questions.statement: An amplifier boosts its $12$-volt input by a factor of $\sqrt{81}$. The output label needs the voltage. What should it read?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{81}=9$, and $12\cdot 9=108$ V. B multiplies by $8$ instead.

blocks.p: A radical asks which number squared (or cubed) gives the inside. Simplify by splitting the inside into a perfect square times a leftover, then root the perfect part. Combine roots only through matching rules.

list: Split first: pull perfect squares out front and leave the rest under the radical.
Multiply or divide freely under one radical; add or subtract only matching radicals.
Squaring undoes a square root — use it to clear radicals from denominators.
Rationalize by multiplying top and bottom by the radical itself.

blocks.p: Roots appear wherever Pythagoras or area runs backward: diagonals, heights, distances, and edges from volumes. Spot the right triangle or the square first, then let the root finish it.

list: A square's diagonal relates to its side by root two; an equilateral height by root three over two.
Coordinate distance is Pythagoras in disguise — square the gaps, add, then root.
Cube edges come from cube roots of volume, never square roots.
Estimate trapped roots between neighboring perfect squares before computing.

questions.statement: A rectangular display measures $40$ cm by $30$ cm. The mount needs the exact diagonal length. What is it?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{40^2+30^2}=\sqrt{2500}=50$ cm — a scaled $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle. D adds the sides.

questions.statement: A square tile's diagonal is $\sqrt{72}$ cm. The installer needs the side length. What is it?
questions.explain: Side $=\sqrt{72}\div\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{36}=6$ cm. Divide under one radical before rooting.

questions.statement: An equilateral triangular sign has sides of $8$ m. Engineering needs its height. What is the height?
questions.explain: Height $=8\sqrt{3}\div 2=4\sqrt{3}$ m. Halving the side but not the root gives A.

questions.statement: A circular pipe's cross-section has area $48\pi$ square cm. What is the inner radius?
questions.explain: $r=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt{3}$ cm after dividing out $\pi$. C is the area coefficient, not the root.

questions.statement: Two gates of a park sit at $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$ on a kilometer grid. How far apart are they?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{(4-1)^2+(6-2)^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$ km. B adds coordinates instead of gaps.

questions.statement: A cubic shipping crate holds $343$ cubic meters. The forklift needs the edge length. What is it?
questions.explain: $\sqrt[3]{343}=7$ m since $7^3=343$. Volume needs a cube root, never a square root.

questions.statement: A cable design calls for a length of $\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}$ meters. The shop needs rationalized form. Which is equivalent?
questions.explain: Multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{2}$: $10\sqrt{2}\div 2=5\sqrt{2}$ m. A forgets to divide.

questions.statement: A framer joins trims of $\sqrt{50}$ m and $\sqrt{18}$ m. What is the combined length in simplest radical form?
questions.explain: $5\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{2}=8\sqrt{2}$ m. Simplify each root first — B's trap adds the insides.

questions.statement: A rectangular mat measures $\sqrt{12}$ m by $\sqrt{3}$ m. What is its area?
questions.explain: Multiply under one radical: $\sqrt{36}=6$. B adds the insides instead of multiplying.

questions.statement: A square photo covers $\frac{16}{25}$ square meters. The frame needs the side length. What is it?
questions.explain: Root top and bottom separately: $4\div 5$ m. D roots only the denominator.

questions.statement: A cubic water tank holds $64$ cubic meters. The plumber needs the edge length for a liner. What is it?
questions.explain: $\sqrt[3]{64}=4$ m. A takes the square root instead of the cube root.

questions.statement: Two square plots have areas $49$ and $81$ square meters. A path will span one side of each end to end. How long is the path?
questions.explain: Sides are $7$ and $9$ m, totaling $16$ m. Root each area first — B's trap roots the sum.

questions.statement: A fence run needs $\sqrt{50}$ meters, about $7.07$ m. The crew has a $7$-m rail. Can it cover the run?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{50}\approx 7.07>7$, so it falls short by about seven centimeters. Rounding down silently fails.

questions.statement: A square tile has sides of $\sqrt{5}$ dm. What is its area?
questions.explain: $(\sqrt{5})^2=5$. Squaring undoes the root — A squares twice.

questions.statement: An optical bench multiplies magnifications of $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{8}$. What is the total magnification?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{2\cdot 8}=\sqrt{16}=4$. Multiply under one radical first.

questions.statement: Eight identical cubic blocks of $27$ cubic cm each are melted into one large cube. What is the new edge length?
questions.explain: Total volume $8\cdot 27=216$ cubic cm, so the edge is $\sqrt[3]{216}=6$ cm. Add volumes first, then take the cube root.

questions.statement: A square field measures $10$ m on each side. The groundskeeper walks the diagonal. How far does she walk?
questions.explain: Diagonal $=10\sqrt{2}$ m. A doubles the side instead of rooting two.

questions.statement: A ladder's feet sit with legs forming a right triangle of sides $1$ m and $2\sqrt{2}$ m. What is the ladder's length?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{1+8}=\sqrt{9}=3$ m. Square each leg first, then add.

questions.statement: A circuit needs wire of length $\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}$ meters. Which rationalized form should the order use?
questions.explain: Multiply by $\sqrt{3}\div\sqrt{3}$: $6\sqrt{3}\div 3=2\sqrt{3}$ m. B skips the division.

questions.statement: A crafter cuts $\sqrt{27}$ m off a $\sqrt{75}$ m ribbon. How much remains, in simplest form?
questions.explain: $5\sqrt{3}-3\sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3}$ m. Simplify before subtracting — A's trap subtracts insides.

questions.statement: A square court tile has sides of $3\sqrt{2}$ m. What area does one tile cover?
questions.explain: $(3\sqrt{2})^2=9\cdot 2=18$. Square the coefficient and the root separately.

questions.statement: A cubic silo holds $1{,}000$ cubic meters of grain. How long is each edge?
questions.explain: $\sqrt[3]{1000}=10$ m. D takes the wrong root.

questions.statement: A square garden bed covers $0.25$ square meters. The edging needs the side length. What is it?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{0.25}=0.5$ m. The root of a decimal smaller than one grows larger — C shrinks it.

questions.statement: A depot at $(0, 0)$ dispatches to a site at $(6, 8)$ on a kilometer grid. What is the straight-line distance?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{36+64}=\sqrt{100}=10$ km — the $6$-$8$-$10$ triangle. A adds the legs.

questions.statement: A $\sqrt{48}$-m rope is cut into pieces each $\sqrt{3}$ m long. How many full pieces result?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{48}\div\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{16}=4$. Divide under one radical. C subtracts insides.

questions.statement: A square mirror has sides of $\sqrt{6}$ m. What is its area?
questions.explain: $(\sqrt{6})^2=6$. B multiplies the root by itself twice over.

questions.statement: A square court measures $9$ m per side. The referee runs corner to corner. How far is that?
questions.explain: Diagonal $=9\sqrt{2}$ m. A doubles instead of rooting.

questions.statement: A border needs $\sqrt{40}$ m of trim, about $6.3$ m. The shop sells $5$-, $6$-, and $7$-m rolls. Which is the smallest that suffices?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{40}$ sits between $6$ and $7$ but above $6$, so only the $7$-m roll covers it.

questions.statement: A receiver reports a squared error of $25$ square meters. The manual needs the actual error radius. What is it?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{25}=5$ m. Root the variance to return to plain units.

questions.statement: A square plot of $72$ square meters is split into two equal squares. What is the side of each new square?
questions.explain: Each half is $36$ square meters, so each side is $\sqrt{36}=6$ m. Halve the area first, then root.

blocks.p: Repeating schedules meet at the least common multiple; cutting into the largest equal pieces uses the greatest common factor. Remainders track what division leaves behind — shift them with the same arithmetic as the numbers.

list: Together-again timing is always an LCM; largest-tile or longest-rope cuts are always a GCF.
Divisibility shortcuts: digit sums for three, last two digits for four, ending digit for five.
Remainders add, subtract, and multiply alongside their numbers — reduce early and often.
Consecutive integers always cover every small factor: any run this long is divisible throughout.

blocks.p: Absolute value measures distance on the number line, so every absolute equation or inequality describes a place, a span, or everything outside one. Translate to distance before solving.

list: Plain bars mean distance from zero; shifted bars mean distance from the shift point.
Equals-a-distance always splits into two symmetric points — never keep just one.
Less-than hugs the inside interval; greater-than escapes to both outside rays.
Equal distance from two points lands exactly on their midpoint.

questions.statement: Two shuttle routes leave a depot together at 8:00 a.m., then repeat every $12$ and $18$ minutes. Dispatch needs the next joint departure. When is it?
questions.explain: Joint departures repeat every $36$ minutes — the LCM of $12$ and $18$. Adding instead of taking the LCM gives B.

questions.statement: A lobby $12$ m by $18$ m needs the largest square tiles that fit with no cutting. What side length should be ordered?
questions.explain: Tile side is $6$ m — the GCF of $12$ and $18$. The LCM answers a timing question, not a cutting one.

questions.statement: A warehouse packs $100$ bulbs into cartons of $7$. How many bulbs are left unpacked?
questions.explain: $100=14\cdot 7+2$, so $2$ remain. The quotient $14$ is not the remainder.

questions.statement: An integer $n$ leaves remainder $3$ when divided by $5$. A coder needs the remainder of $n+2$ upon division by $5$. What is it?
questions.explain: $3+2=5\equiv 0\pmod 5$. Remainders shift with the number — reduce the sum.

questions.statement: A lock uses a prime combination strictly between $20$ and $30$. How many choices exist?
questions.explain: Only $23$ and $29$ qualify — $2$ choices. $25$ and $27$ fall to small factors.

questions.statement: A gear has $2^4\cdot 3^2$ teeth positions, and engineering counts its positive divisors for a meshing table. How many are there?
questions.explain: Add one to each exponent and multiply: $(4+1)(2+1)=15$. Multiplying raw exponents gives B.

questions.statement: A serial number ends with the units digit of $2^{30}$. The units digits of powers of two cycle through $2$, $4$, $8$, $6$. What is the digit?
questions.explain: $30\div 4$ leaves remainder $2$, so take the second in the cycle: $4$.

questions.statement: An oven must hold $150$ degrees within $8$ degrees. An inspector writes the acceptable range. Which range is correct?
questions.explain: $|T-150|\le 8$ means $142\le T\le 158$. One-sided options miss half the interval.

questions.statement: A drone drops $12$ m below its launch pad, then climbs to $7$ m above it. What is the total vertical distance traveled?
questions.explain: $|-12|+|7|=12+7=19$ m. Net displacement ($5$ m) is not distance traveled.

questions.statement: Three consecutive integers sum to $105$. A puzzle asks for the largest. What is it?
questions.explain: The middle equals the average ($35$), so the largest is $36$. Dividing by three finds the middle, not the end.

questions.statement: For integers $m$ and $n$, which expression is always even?
questions.explain: A factor of $2$ outside guarantees evenness regardless of $m,n$. The rest depend on parity.

questions.statement: Raffle tickets numbered below $50$ win if divisible by both $3$ and $4$. How many winning numbers exist?
questions.explain: Divisible by both means divisible by $12$: $12$, $24$, $36$, $48$ — four numbers.

questions.statement: Ropes of $48$ m and $180$ m must be cut into the longest equal pieces with nothing left. How long is each piece?
questions.explain: The GCF of $48$ and $180$ is $12$ m. A divides only one rope evenly.

questions.statement: Two beacons flash every $8$ and $12$ seconds starting together. A sailor counts seconds until the next joint flash. How many?
questions.explain: The LCM of $8$ and $12$ is $24$ s. Adding the periods answers a different question.

questions.statement: A quiz asks which of these is prime: $91, 93, 95, 97$. Which should be circled?
questions.explain: $91=7\cdot 13$, $93=3\cdot 31$, $95=5\cdot 19$ — only $97$ survives. Test small primes first.

questions.statement: An amphitheater fills rows $1$ through $50$ with one more seat than the row number ($2$ seats in row $1$, up to $51$ in row $50$). What is the total capacity?
questions.explain: Sum $2$ through $51$: $(2+51)\cdot 50\div 2=1325$. Pair first-plus-last, then multiply by half the count.

questions.statement: A sensor trips when the distance between $2x$ and $6$ equals $10$. The technician needs the positive setting. What is $x$?
questions.explain: $|2x-6|=10$ gives $2x=16$ or $2x=-4$; the positive root is $8$.

questions.statement: A two-digit number plus its reversal equals $121$. How many such numbers exist?
questions.explain: Digit sum must be $11$: pairs $2$–$9$ through $9$–$2$ — eight numbers. The tens digit cannot be zero.

questions.statement: The product of any three consecutive positive integers is always divisible by which number?
questions.explain: Every run of three covers a multiple of $3$ and an even number, so $6$ always divides it.

questions.statement: A coder needs $3^{10}$ modulo $4$ for a hash check. Even powers of $3$ leave remainder $1$. What is the remainder?
questions.explain: $3^2=9\equiv 1\pmod 4$, so $(3^2)^5\equiv 1$. Reduce the base power first.

questions.statement: A part passes when $|x+3|>5$. Quality writes the passing set. Which describes it?
questions.explain: Greater-than escapes both rays: $x+3>5$ or $x+3<-5$. A describes the failing inside.

questions.statement: A combinatorics result equals $100!$ and the report needs its trailing zeros. How many are there?
questions.explain: Count factors of five: $20+4=24$. Each zero needs a $2$–$5$ pair, and fives are scarce.

questions.statement: A recipe scales to any whole serving that divides evenly into batches of $2$ through $6$. What is the smallest batch size?
questions.explain: $\text{LCM}(1,\dots,6)=60$. B multiplies everything without removing overlaps.

questions.statement: A two-digit number has digits summing to $9$, and subtracting $27$ reverses its digits. What is the number?
A lottery draws odd multiples of $5$ below $100$. How many possible draws exist?
questions.explain: They run $5$, $15$, and so on through $95$ — ten numbers. Halve the twenty multiples of five.

questions.statement: A marker must sit where $|x-10|=|x-2|$, equidistant from exits at $10$ and $2$. Where should it go?
questions.explain: Equal distances meet at the midpoint: $(10+2)\div 2=6$.

questions.statement: A parts bin holds $72=2^3\cdot 3^2$ bolts per kit. How many positive divisors does $72$ have?
questions.explain: $(3+1)(2+1)=12$. The exponent sum ($5$) is not the divisor count.

questions.statement: Two machines beep every $15$ and $20$ minutes from a joint beep at noon. When is the next joint beep?
questions.explain: The LCM of $15$ and $20$ is $60$ minutes, so $1{:}00$ p.m. Adding gives $12{:}35$, wrongly.

questions.statement: A checksum needs $2^{50}$ modulo $3$. Since $2\equiv -1\pmod 3$, what is the remainder?
questions.explain: $(-1)^{50}=1$. Even exponents erase the sign.

questions.statement: Four consecutive even integers sum to $100$. The invoices need the largest. What is it?
questions.explain: Average $25$ sits between $24$ and $26$, so the run is $22$, $24$, $26$, $28$. Largest: $28$.

blocks.p: Complex numbers extend the line into a plane: a real part plus an imaginary part built on $i$. Every higher power of $i$ collapses through its defining square, so no exponent ever survives unreduced.

list: Collapse $i^2$ into its value first, before any other arithmetic.
Powers of $i$ cycle every four — reduce the exponent modulo four and read the remainder.
Adding or subtracting combines real with real and imaginary with imaginary, separately.
Multiplying works like binomials (FOIL), then collapse every squared $i$.

blocks.p: The conjugate mirrors a number across the real axis, and the modulus measures its distance from the origin. Together they turn division into multiplication and size into Pythagoras.

list: Conjugating flips only the imaginary sign; the real part never moves.
A number times its conjugate is always real — a sum of two squares.
Modulus is the hypotenuse over the real and imaginary legs.
To divide, multiply top and bottom by the bottom's conjugate.

questions.statement: A signal model rotates phase by powers of $i$, cycling $i,-1,-i,1$. A filter applies the factor $i^{23}$. What is the resulting factor?
questions.explain: $23\div 4$ leaves remainder $3$, and $i^3=-i$. Reduce the exponent first.

questions.statement: Two circuit elements in series have impedances $(3+2i)$ and $(5-7i)$ ohms. The total impedance is their sum. What is it?
questions.explain: Combine real with real and imaginary with imaginary: $8-5i$. D multiplies instead of adding.

questions.statement: A calibration subtracts a reference $(2+5i)$ from a reading $(6+i)$. What is the corrected value?
questions.explain: $(6-2)+(1-5)i=4-4i$. Distribute the minus to both parts of the reference.

questions.statement: An amplifier chain multiplies gains $(2+3i)$ and $(1-i)$. What is the combined gain?
questions.explain: FOIL: $2-2i+3i-3i^2=2+i+3=5+i$. Forgetting that $i^2=-1$ gives A.

questions.statement: A power calculation contains the term $14i^2$. The report needs its real value. What is it?
questions.explain: $14\cdot(-1)=-14$. The $i$ disappears entirely once squared.

questions.statement: A receiver with impedance $5-3i$ ohms needs its complex conjugate for maximum power transfer. What impedance should be attached?
questions.explain: Flip only the imaginary sign: $5+3i$. Negating both parts gives D.

questions.statement: A fault current is modeled as $3+4i$ amps. Protective gear is rated by its modulus. What is the magnitude?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{9+16}=5$ amps — the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle. C forgets the final root.

questions.statement: A control loop multiplies corrections $(4i)$ and $(3i)$. What is the resulting real factor?
questions.explain: $12i^2=-12$. Two imaginary factors make a real (negative) product.

questions.statement: A formula calls for $\frac{1}{i}$. The codebase needs it in $a+bi$ form. What is it?
questions.explain: Multiply by $i\div i$: $i\div i^2=i\div(-1)=-i$. A drops the sign.

questions.statement: A sensor's output power equals $|2+i|^2$. What power does the display show?
questions.explain: $(2+i)(2-i)=4+1=5$. Conjugate pairs multiply to a sum of squares.

questions.statement: A clocking signal uses $i^{40}$. What does it simplify to?
A filter squares the tap $(1+i)$. What is the result?
questions.explain: $1+2i+i^2=2i$. The real parts cancel through $i^2=-1$.

questions.statement: A mixer adds $(5+2i)$ and subtracts $(3+2i)$. What remains?
questions.explain: Imaginary parts cancel: $(5-3)+(2-2)i=2$.

questions.statement: A $3$-ohm resistor carries current $(2+i)$ amps. By Ohm's law $V=IZ$, what is the voltage?
questions.explain: Distribute the real $3$: $6+3i$ volts. C multiplies only the real part.

questions.statement: A bridge balances $(7-i)$ against $(-7+i)$. What is their sum?
questions.explain: Opposites annihilate: $(7-7)+(-1+1)i=0$.

questions.statement: A routine evaluates $i^3+i^4$. What value should the test expect?
questions.explain: $-i+1=1-i$. Reduce each power through the four-cycle separately.

questions.statement: A coil factor of $(3i)$ is squared in an energy formula. What is the result?
questions.explain: $9i^2=-9$. Square the coefficient and collapse the $i^2$.

questions.statement: A phasor is $-5+12i$. Its magnitude sets a breaker rating. What is it?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=13$. Signs vanish inside the squares.

questions.statement: A reading of $(10+5i)$ is averaged over $5$ samples. What is the per-sample value?
questions.explain: Divide both parts: $2+i$. A divides only the real part.

questions.statement: A drift of $(6-2i)$ is split equally between two channels. What does each channel carry?
questions.explain: Halve real and imaginary alike: $3-i$.

questions.statement: Two stages with gains $(1+2i)$ and $(3+i)$ cascade. What is the total gain?
questions.explain: $3+i+6i+2i^2=3+7i-2=1+7i$. Collect the $i^2$ into the real total.

questions.statement: A matched filter multiplies $(4-3i)$ by its conjugate. What is the output?
questions.explain: $16+9=25$ — always a sum of squares, always real.

questions.statement: A log sums $i^7$ and $i^8$. What total should appear?
questions.explain: $i^7=-i$ and $i^8=1$, totaling $1-i$.

questions.statement: An error $(9-4i)$ is corrected by $(9-i)$. What residual remains?
questions.explain: Real parts cancel ($0$); imaginary: $-4-(-1)=-3$, so $-3i$.

questions.statement: A transmission phasor reads $8-6i$ kV. What is its magnitude?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{64+36}=10$ kV — the scaled $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle.

questions.statement: Multiplying by $i$ rotates a phasor $90$ degrees. Starting from $(3+i)$, what is one rotation's result?
questions.explain: $3i+i^2=-1+3i$. Rotation swaps the parts with a sign flip.

questions.statement: A detector multiplies $(5i)$ by $(-2i)$. What does it register?
questions.explain: $-10i^2=10$. Two imaginary factors with opposite signs go positive real.

questions.statement: Loads of $(3+4i)$ and $(-3+2i)$ ohms combine in series. What is the total?
questions.explain: Real parts cancel ($0$); imaginary sums to $6i$.

questions.statement: A stability check evaluates $i^{50}$. What value should the assertion use?
questions.explain: $i^{50}=(i^4)^{12}\cdot i^2=-1$. Strip full cycles, then read the remainder.

questions.statement: Two probes read $(2+3i)$ and $(5+i)$. The display shows the modulus of their difference. What appears?
questions.explain: Difference is $-3+2i$ with modulus $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$.

blocks.p: A matrix is a table, and its size (rows by columns) decides everything. Addition, subtraction, and scalar moves all work entry by entry — but only tables of identical shape may combine.

list: Read size as rows-by-columns before any operation; mismatched shapes cannot add or subtract.
Adding or subtracting pairs up matching seats — never mix positions.
A scalar multiplies every single entry; nothing is exempt.
Zero tables change nothing; identity tables preserve whatever they touch.

blocks.p: Matrix multiplication chains tables together: each new entry is a row-times-column total. Cost tables times quantity columns are products in disguise, and two-by-two determinants collapse to one diagonal minus the other.

list: Inner sizes must agree — the outer sizes give the answer's shape.
Each entry is a row-times-column sum; order matters, so products rarely commute.
Price-by-quantity and rate-by-time tables multiply exactly this way.
Point moves (flips and turns) remap coordinates by fixed rules.

questions.statement: Two depots report stock as $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8\end{pmatrix}$. What is the combined stock matrix?
questions.explain: Add matching seats: $1+5$, $2+6$, $3+7$, $4+8$. D adds along diagonals only.

questions.statement: Morning and afternoon sales tables are $\begin{pmatrix}10 & 20 \\ 15 & 25\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}5 & 10 \\ 10 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. What is the day total?
questions.explain: Entrywise sums give $15,30,25,30$. B multiplies instead of adding.

questions.statement: A recipe matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ is tripled for catering. What is the scaled matrix?
questions.explain: The scalar hits every entry: $6,-3,0,12$. B scales only part of the table.

questions.statement: A two-stage process multiplies $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ by $B=\begin{pmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8\end{pmatrix}$. What is $AB$?
questions.explain: Row-times-column sums: $5+14$, $6+16$, $15+28$, $18+32$. B multiplies entrywise instead.

questions.statement: A timetable $A$ is $2\times 3$ and a roster $B$ is $3\times 2$. An analyst forms $AB$. What size is the result?
questions.explain: Inner threes agree; outer sizes give $2\times 2$. D confuses this with the reverse order.

questions.statement: Tables $A$ ($2\times 3$) and $C$ ($2\times 3$) track two regions. A report requests $AC$. What happens?
questions.explain: Inner sizes $3$ versus $2$ never meet, so $AC$ does not exist. Shapes must chain.

questions.statement: A kit uses $4$ bolts at $9$ and $6$ washers at $14$. Purchasing models this as $[9,14]$ times $[4,6]^T$. What is the kit cost?
questions.explain: $9\cdot 4+14\cdot 6=36+84=120$. A adds everything without weighting.

questions.statement: Two stores price three goods as rows $[4,7,10]$ and $[5,6,9]$, selling $[3,2,5]^T$ units of each. What is store A's revenue?
questions.explain: $4\cdot 3+7\cdot 2+10\cdot 5=12+14+50=76$. B is store B's total — read the right row.

questions.statement: A calibration factor is $\det\begin{pmatrix}4 & 7 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. What is its value?
questions.explain: $4\cdot 5-7\cdot 2=20-14=6$. A adds the diagonals instead of subtracting.

questions.statement: A map transform has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 4 & 9\end{pmatrix}$. Its area scale is the determinant. What is it?
questions.explain: $6\cdot 9-3\cdot 4=54-12=42$. Order matters: main diagonal first.

questions.statement: A sensor at $(3,-2)$ is mirrored across the $y$-axis. What are the new coordinates?
questions.explain: Mirroring across the $y$-axis flips only $x$: $(-3,-2)$. A flips the wrong axis.

questions.statement: A drone waypoint $(4,1)$ rotates $90$ degrees counterclockwise about the origin. Where does it land?
questions.explain: A quarter turn maps $(x,y)$ to $(-y,x)$: $(-1,4)$. D turns clockwise instead.

questions.statement: Stock $\begin{pmatrix}9 & 8 \\ 7 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ minus usage $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ leaves what?
questions.explain: Subtract seat by seat — every entry drops by an equal step here. A adds instead.

questions.statement: A ledger $A$ is adjusted by the zero table $Z$. What is $A+Z$?
questions.explain: Zero changes nothing entrywise, so the ledger stands. Sizes already agree.

questions.statement: Scores $[2,5,1]$ carry weights $[3,4,6]^T$. What is the weighted total?
questions.explain: $2\cdot 3+5\cdot 4+1\cdot 6=6+20+6=32$. Pair each score with its own weight.

questions.statement: A route matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ acts on stop vector $\begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 5\end{pmatrix}$. What is the result?
questions.explain: Row sums: $2\cdot 4+1\cdot 5=13$ and $0\cdot 4+3\cdot 5=15$.

questions.statement: Ticket prices $[12,7]$ meet counts $\begin{pmatrix}100 & 60 \\ 150 & 80\end{pmatrix}$ (Friday row, Saturday row; adult, child). What is Saturday's revenue?
questions.explain: Saturday row: $150\cdot 12+80\cdot 7=1800+560=2360$. A is Friday's total.

questions.statement: An audit code equals $\det\begin{pmatrix}10 & 4 \\ 5 & 11\end{pmatrix}$. What is the code?
A formula table $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ is doubled. What is the new table?
questions.explain: Every entry doubles. A doubles only the diagonal.

questions.statement: A marker at $(2,5)$ reflects across the $x$-axis. Where does it appear?
questions.explain: Reflecting across the $x$-axis flips only $y$.

questions.statement: A swap matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ acts on $\begin{pmatrix}7 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$. What comes out?
questions.explain: Rows trade places: the top becomes $3$, the bottom $7$. Order of rows is order of outputs.

questions.statement: The identity $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ multiplies $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 9 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. What results?
questions.explain: Identity preserves every entry. B zeroes the off-diagonal instead.

questions.statement: Loads $[6,2,9]$ meet rates $[1,3,2]^T$. What is the combined total?
A shear factor is $\det\begin{pmatrix}3 & 8 \\ 4 & 6\end{pmatrix}$. What is it?
questions.explain: $3\cdot 6-8\cdot 4=18-32=-14$. Keep the subtraction order: main diagonal minus the other.

questions.statement: Shelves hold $\begin{pmatrix}50 & 30 \\ 20 & 40\end{pmatrix}$ and sell $\begin{pmatrix}12 & 8 \\ 5 & 15\end{pmatrix}$. What remains?
questions.explain: Subtract per shelf and product. D multiplies the tables instead.

questions.statement: A camera at $(3,-4)$ pans $180$ degrees about the origin. Where does it point?
questions.explain: A half turn negates both coordinates: $(-3,4)$. A swaps instead of negating.

questions.statement: A planner multiplies $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ by $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7\end{pmatrix}$. What is the product?
questions.explain: Row-times-column: $8,10,22,26$. A multiplies entrywise — never legal for products.

questions.statement: Weights $[0.3,0.5,0.2]$ meet scores $[80,90,70]^T$. What is the final grade?
questions.explain: $0.3(80)+0.5(90)+0.2(70)=24+45+14=83$. Weights must pair with their own scores.

questions.statement: A code equals $\det\begin{pmatrix}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$. What is it?
questions.explain: $(-2)(4)-(5)(3)=-8-15=-23$. Signs ride along inside the diagonals.

questions.statement: A model needs $2A-B$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 5 \\ 0 & 4\end{pmatrix}$. What is the result?
questions.explain: Scale first ($8,2,4,6$), then subtract ($6,-3,4,2$). Scaling after subtracting misplaces the weights.

blocks.p: A vector is a trip ticket: horizontal steps plus vertical steps. Adding trips chains them tip to tail, component by component; scaling stretches every step of the ticket equally.

list: Read components as signed steps — negatives walk backward along that axis.
Add or subtract matching components only; never cross the axes.
A scalar reaches every component; a negative scalar also reverses direction.
Equal-and-opposite trips cancel to the zero ticket.

blocks.math: \langle a,b\rangle\pm\langle c,d\rangle=\langle a\pm c,b\pm d\rangle \qquad c\langle a,b\rangle=\langle ca,cb\rangle

blocks.p: Size comes from Pythagoras on the components, and the dot product tests teamwork: matching directions add up (work is force dotted with distance), while a zero dot means a perfect right angle.

list: Magnitude roots the sum of squared components — signs vanish inside.
Unit tickets come from dividing a vector by its own length.
Dot products multiply matches and add: parallel teamwork scores highest.
A zero dot product certifies perpendicular paths, no protractor needed.

questions.statement: A hiker walks $\langle 3,4\rangle$ km, then $\langle 1,-2\rangle$ km. What is the total displacement vector?
questions.explain: Add matching components: $3+1$ and $4-2$. Trips chain tip to tail.

questions.statement: A patrol route is the vector $\langle 6,8\rangle$ km. How long is the patrol?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{36+64}=10$ km — the $6$-$8$-$10$ triangle. A adds the legs.

questions.statement: A tug pulls with force $\langle 2,-5\rangle$ kN, then triples its effort in the same direction. What is the new force vector?
questions.explain: The scalar reaches both components: $\langle 6,-15\rangle$. B scales only the first.

questions.statement: A crate slides $\langle 9,7\rangle$ m, then back $\langle 4,3\rangle$ m. What is the net displacement?
questions.explain: Subtract per axis: $9-4$ and $7-3$. A adds the return trip instead.

questions.statement: A force $\langle 2,3\rangle$ N moves a load $\langle 4,-1\rangle$ m. Work equals the dot product. How much work is done?
questions.explain: $2\cdot 4+3\cdot(-1)=8-3=5$ J. Match, multiply, then add.

questions.statement: A compass heading follows $\langle 3,4\rangle$. What is the unit vector in that direction?
questions.explain: Length is $5$, so divide each part: $\langle 3/5,4/5\rangle$. D inverts instead of normalizing.

questions.statement: A cable runs along $\langle 5,12\rangle$ m. How much cable is needed?
A plane flies $\langle 400,0\rangle$ km/h through wind $\langle 0,50\rangle$ km/h. What is the ground speed?
questions.explain: Resultant $\langle 400,50\rangle$ with length $\sqrt{162500}\approx 403$ km/h. A adds the speeds directly.

questions.statement: A force $\langle 10,5\rangle$ N pushes a cart along $\langle 6,2\rangle$ m. How much work results?
questions.explain: $10\cdot 6+5\cdot 2=70$ J. Dots measure teamwork, not totals.

questions.statement: Two guide wires run along $\langle 2,3\rangle$ and $\langle -3,2\rangle$. Are they perpendicular?
questions.explain: $2(-3)+3(2)=0$ certifies a right angle with no protractor.

questions.statement: A tether follows $\langle -9,12\rangle$ m. What is its length?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{81+144}=15$ m. Signs vanish inside the squares.

questions.statement: A robot obeys $2\langle 4,-1\rangle-\langle 3,5\rangle$. What single move results?
questions.explain: Scale first ($\langle 8,-2\rangle$), then subtract: $\langle 5,-7\rangle$.

questions.statement: A heading $\langle 3,4\rangle$ makes an angle $\theta$ above the $x$-axis with $\tan\theta=4/3$. About how many degrees is that?
questions.explain: A $3$-$4$-$5$ slope tilts about $53^\circ$. The complement ($37^\circ$) measures from the $y$-axis.

questions.statement: A $10$-N wind blows at $30^\circ$ above the $x$-axis. Its $y$-component is $10\sin 30^\circ$. What is it?
questions.explain: $10\cdot 0.5=5$ N climbs vertically. A is the $x$-component.

questions.statement: A ferry aims $\langle 0,12\rangle$ km/h across a current of $\langle 5,0\rangle$ km/h. How fast does it travel over ground?
questions.explain: Resultant $\langle 5,12\rangle$ has length $13$ km/h. A adds speeds from different axes.

questions.statement: A navigation check dots $\langle 5,-2\rangle$ with $\langle 3,4\rangle$. What is the result?
questions.explain: $15-8=7$. Dots collapse to a single number, never a vector.

questions.statement: A drone flies $\langle 4,-4\rangle$ km out and $\langle -4,4\rangle$ km back. What is the total displacement?
questions.explain: Equal-and-opposite legs cancel to the zero vector. A adds magnitudes instead.

questions.statement: A cable drops along $\langle 7,24\rangle$ m. How much cable is used?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{49+576}=25$ m — the $7$-$24$-$25$ triangle. C stops before rooting.

questions.statement: A survey halves the vector $\langle 10,-6\rangle$ for a finer grid. What is the new vector?
questions.explain: Halve both components alike. Partial scaling bends the direction.

questions.statement: A courier covers $\langle 1,1\rangle$, then $\langle 2,3\rangle$, then $\langle -1,2\rangle$ km. What is the net displacement?
A trail combines $\langle 2,-3\rangle$ and $\langle -2,3\rangle$ km. What is the loop's net length from start?
questions.explain: Opposites cancel: $\langle 0,0\rangle$, so length $0$. C measures one leg only.

questions.statement: A probe descends along $\langle 0,-8\rangle$ m/s. What is the unit vector of its motion?
questions.explain: Length $8$; dividing gives straight down with length one.

questions.statement: A force $\langle 3,4\rangle$ N acts over displacement $\langle 5,0\rangle$ m. How much work is done?
questions.explain: $3\cdot 5+4\cdot 0=15$ J. Only the aligned part works.

questions.statement: Paths along $\langle 1,0\rangle$ and $\langle 1,1\rangle$ meet at a junction. Their dot is $1$ and lengths are $1$ and $\sqrt{2}$. What is the angle between them?
questions.explain: $\cos\theta=1\div\sqrt{2}$, so $\theta=45^\circ$. The diagonal splits the right angle.

questions.statement: Two tugs pull $\langle 6,2\rangle$ and $\langle -2,4\rangle$ kN on one barge. What is the combined pull's magnitude?
questions.explain: Sum $\langle 4,6\rangle$ first, then $\sqrt{16+36}=\sqrt{52}$ kN. Never root before adding.

questions.statement: A survey takes $\langle -2,5\rangle$ minus $\langle 3,-1\rangle$. What vector remains?
questions.explain: $-2-3$ and $5-(-1)$: $\langle -5,6\rangle$. Subtracting a negative adds.

questions.statement: A gust quadruples the vector $\langle -1,2\rangle$. What is the result?
questions.explain: Scale both parts: $\langle -4,8\rangle$. D also flips the signs.

questions.statement: Two edges run $\langle 4,1\rangle$ and $\langle -1,4\rangle$. Do they meet at a right angle?
questions.explain: $4(-1)+1(4)=0$ — perpendicular. A misplaces a sign.

questions.statement: A ball rolls with velocity $\langle -6,-8\rangle$ m/s. What is its speed?
questions.explain: $\sqrt{36+64}=10$ m/s. Direction never changes speed.

questions.statement: A launcher fires at $20$ m/s, $60^\circ$ above east. The east component is $20\cos 60^\circ$. What is it?
questions.explain: $20\cdot 0.5=10$ m/s eastward. A is the north component.

blocks.p: Linear equations hide the unknown behind reversible moves. Name the variable, translate each sentence into one expression, then undo operations in reverse order until it stands alone.

list: Clear fractions first by multiplying every term by the common denominator.
Distribute across parentheses before collecting like terms together.
Move variable terms to one side and constants to the other, then divide.
Check by plugging the answer back into the original story.

blocks.p: Formulas are equations wearing many letters: pick the target, treat everything else as a plain number, and isolate step by step. Word models — ages, coins, perimeters, mixtures — all reduce to sums set equal.
